To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Rift Valley fever (RFV) virus is endemic in both buffalo and domestic cattle populations in the northern part of Botswana and that the seroprevalences of the two species differ.

Rift Valley Fever virus (RVF) neutralizing antibodies were detected in 12.7 % (95% confidence intervals [CI] 7.8-19.5%) and 5.7 % (4.3-7.5%) respectively, of African buffalo and domestic cattle sampled at the interface of livestock areas and the wildlife reserves of Chobe National Park and Okavango Delta in Northern Botswana, with the overall prevalence being significantly higher for buffalo than for cattle.

1) RVF virus circulation has been documented in cattle and buffalo in Northern Botswana; 2) the prevalence of antibodies against RVF virus was significantly higher in buffalo compared with cattle; 3) the prevalence of anti-RVFV antibodies was significantly higher in the Chobe National park compared with the Okavango delta.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the ecology of Rift Valley fever virus (RVF) in Botswana.
the ecology of Rift Valley fever ( RVF ) and its vectors in Africa, with a specific focus on the ecology of the virus and its vectors in Botswana.
the serological evidence of Rift Valley Fever virus circulation in domestic cattle and African buffalo in Northern Botswana.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the seroprevalences of RVF virus antibodies in cattle and buffalo were higher in CNP (9.5%) than in OD (4%), and higher in buffalo (12.7%) than in cattle (5.7%) in Northern Botswana.

the data presented in this study provide the first serological evidence of RVFV circulation in both domestic and wild ruminants in Botswana, which could have significant implications on the risk of RVFV introduction into Botswana from neighbouring countries and the possible emergence and spread of this zoonosis in this region.
RVF virus circulation is widespread in the region and that it affects domestic animals and wildlife.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the prevalence of RVFV was significantly different among the two wildlife areas (CNP and OD) for the two species (buffalo and cattle).
RVF is endemic in Botswana, with a higher prevalence in buffalo and in the Chobe National park.
RVF virus is endemic in Botswana and that there is a high potential of transmission from wildlife to domestic animals and vice versa.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a need to increase surveillance of RVFV at the interface between wildlife and livestock in Botswana and to develop a national plan for RVF prevention and control.
RVFV circulation is not limited to the livestock areas, but it also occurs in wildlife areas, and that cattle and wildlife are both involved in the epidemiology of RVF in Botswana.
RVF is endemic in Botswana, and the risk for human infection is high.
